chapter_note: This chapter contains zero substrate cosmological-correspondential teaching. Teaching purity is 0.000. The entire chapter is apostolic narrative — Mani's missionary journeys through India, Persia, Mesene, Babylon, and Media/Parthia, his repeated summons by King Shapur, and opposition from authorities in various lands. It includes a near-verbatim NT citation (John 3:19-20) repeated twice (¶7, ¶11). The chapter is framed by a disciple's request for 'two Manis' and closes with exhortation (¶25) and devotional response (¶26). This is purely institutional material — biographical, hagiographic, and historically situated — with no cosmic mappings, no correspondential architecture, and no trace of the oldest teaching layer.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Apostolic narrative setup with historical proper nouns (Ktesiphon, Shapur) and honorific titles ('our master Manichaios, our light enlightener'). High institutional score (28.26). Classic institutional layer: Mani's historical context, kings, cities.
Continuation of Shapur narrative. 'He spoke with him and proclaimed to him the word of God' — apostolic mission language. 'Congregation' is institutional vocabulary.
Third iteration of Shapur summoning pattern. Purely narrative, no cosmological content.

Disciple Aurades son of Kapelos — historical proper names firmly anchor this to the institutional layer. The 'two Manis' request is a narrative device, not a cosmological question. Dialogue frame vocabulary present ('our enlightener', 'our master') but embedded in apostolic narrative.

Mani's response: 'I, a single Mani, came to the world to proclaim in it the word of God.' Apostolic self-description. 'Our enlightener' is hagiographic. 'The good will that had been entrusted to me' — mission language.
Continuation of Mani's speech about his inability to speak freely. 'The will of the mystery, which I preach in the living truth' — missionary/apostolic language, not cosmic mapping.

Contains near-verbatim NT citation: 'the world loves the darkness; but it hates the light, because its works are evil' (John 3:19-20). 'Its sects' references contemporary religious landscape. Entirely apostolic narrative about opposition to Mani's preaching.
Heavily lacunose transitional paragraph. Mani continues addressing the disciple. 'Recount it to you' — narrative speech act.
Mani's sea voyage to India — biographical/apostolic narrative. 'I stirred the whole land of India' — missionary journey account. Heavily damaged but clearly historical.
Mani ceasing to speak freely — biographical detail. 'The voice that is of truth, which is entrusted to me' — mission commissioning language.

Difficulties in India. References to 'counsellors, satraps, governors' — contemporary political structures. Repeats the John 3:19 citation: 'the world loves the darkness; but it hates the light.' Heavily damaged.
Journey from India to Persia. Geographic proper nouns (India, Persia). 'Powers and authorities' — contemporary political structures. Heavily lacunose apostolic narrative.
Extremely fragmentary. References 'the Father' and 'their land' — too damaged for confident analysis but consistent with apostolic narrative context.

Rhetorical pattern: the land tolerates kings, satraps, governors — but not Mani's truth. This is a recurring argumentative structure in the chapter (repeated in ¶16, ¶19, ¶20). Contemporary political vocabulary.

Journey to Mesene. 'I separated the light from the darkness and discriminated life from death' — though this SOUNDS cosmological, it describes Mani's preaching activity ('I proclaimed'), not cosmic process. The 'commandments' reference confirms institutional context.

Opposition in Mesene. 'Ruling-power and swarm of demons' — Mani interprets opposition demonologically. 'Kings, caesars, satraps, governors' — contemporary political structures. 'The voice of life that I cried out among them' — missionary language.
Journey to Babylon/land of Assyrians. Geographic proper nouns. Same missionary vocabulary: 'word of truth and life', 'separated the light from the darkness.' Apostolic narrative.

Opposition in Babylon. 'Sects', 'lawless judges', 'rulers', 'leaders' — contemporary social structures. 'Protection of the Father' — theological claim about divine aid. Direct address 'as you yourselves see' — addresses the listening community.

Rhetorical argument about Assyria: tolerates kings, eparchs, generals, caesars, governors — but not Mani. Same recurring pattern as ¶14, ¶16. Political vocabulary. 'I left behind me the Assyrians' — biographical.
Journey to Medes and Parthians. 'I played the harp of wisdom' — poetic missionary metaphor. Same rhetorical pattern: the land accepts kings and leaders but not Mani's truth. Geographic proper nouns.

Opens with dialogue frame formula 'Then the apostle speaks to that disciple' but the entire content is apostolic narrative — Mani summarizing his mission. 'I have subdued its powers', 'I have planted', 'I have sown this seed of life' — missionary language. No cosmological teaching to extract.
Climactic rhetorical argument: 'if two Manis had come to the world, what place would be able to tolerate them?' Answers the disciple's request from ¶4. Purely narrative/apostolic.
'Walking on tip-toes' — vivid image of Mani's precarious position. Biographical/autobiographical. No cosmological content.
Transitions toward closing. 'All of you, pray to God' — direct address to community. 'Holy church' — institutional vocabulary. Bridges from narrative to exhortation.

Classic exhortation closure: 'blessed are you if you make yourselves strong in this truth' — beatitude formula, direct address, moral injunction. 'The life which continues for ever and ever' — eschatological promise. Standard devotional wrapper.

Disciple's devotional response within the narrative frame. 'Blessed am I my master' uses beatitude language but within apostolic narrative. References to 'the Father who sent you', 'God who has sent you' — apostolic commissioning theology. 'Your advent to us' — hagiographic. The whole paragraph serves as institutional-devotional closure to the chapter.
